text:
Richard Stallman was born in New York City on March 16, 1953, into a Jewish family. He developed an early interest in computers, starting by reading IBM 7094 manuals as a pre-teen. He studied at Columbia University and later worked as a programmer at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, where he gained renown in the hacker community, often known by his initials, RMS.
The fragmentation of hacker culture in the late 1970s and early 1980s, marked by manufacturers restricting source code and using restrictive licenses, led Stallman to proclaim the blocking of user freedom as a "crime against humanity." In February 1984, he quit his MIT job to work full-time on the GNU project. He published the GNU Manifesto in 1985, outlining his motivation for creating the free operating system GNU, which was compatible with Unix. He popularized the concept of copyleft, first implementing it in the GNU Emacs General Public License, and later releasing the GNU General Public License (GPL) in 1989. Stallman is an outspoken political campaigner for the free software movement, advocating for software freedom over proprietary software.
